title: Pauly Shore Bringing Newest Special ‘Road Comic: Live From Portland’ To PlayStation 5 In November
full_text: Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt Chase Sui Wonders In Talks to Join A24’s ‘Goblin’ ‘Widow’s Bay’ Breakout Kate O’Flynn Joins Olivia Wilde Comedy ‘Naughty’ At Universal; Jamie Demetriou & Dexter Sol Ansell Also Set Jay Roach Producing Female-Driven Ensemble Comedy For New Line From ‘Fockers’ Collaborator Larry Stuckey And Joanna Leeds View All October 30, 2026 8:41am Add us as a Google Preferred Source EXCLUSIVE: Comedian Pauly Shore is set to release a new half-hour stand-up special, Road Comic: Live from Portland , via PlayStation 5 on November 1. Shore’s special is one of the first ever made available for free on-demand viewing via Live TV streaming on the gaming console, joining recent specials from the likes of Jeremiah Watkins, Jack Jr. and Paul Virzi. Live TV marks a departure from earlier viewing options: Previously, the options for PlayStation users were either to purchase specials through the PlayStation Store — something Sony discontinued for all film/TV in 2021 — or stream through third-party apps such as YouTube. Related Stories News Comedy Central Returns To Full-Length Specials With Chloe Radcliffe's 'Eyes Down Here' News Janine Harouni Dates New YouTube Stand-Up Special 'Man'oushe' In his new special, Shore gets personal — messing with the audience, looking back on being raised by comedians at the legendary Comedy Store, reminiscing about his former co-stars, opening up about health scares and getting into his beef with Will Ferrell at Equinox. Check out a trailer above. Watch on Deadline Shore taped the special at the Portland Helium Comedy Club in Portland, OR and will release it on his YouTube page on November 17. He lists Ronald McDonald and Burger King as the producers of his special, with Taco Bell as its executive producer; probably take those credits with a grain of salt. He directed the half-hour himself, with Comedy Compound Productions and Robot Pirate Media as the production companies involved. Born into comedy — the son of comedian Sammy Shore and longtime Comedy Store owner Mitzi Shore — Pauly has now been performing stand-up for nearly four decades. He broke out via his MTV show Totally Pauly , which ran for six years, before going on to roles in iconic ’90s comedies like Bio Dome and Encino Man , and starring in and producing his own projects, like Pauly Shore Is Dead . Over the years, he’s released myriad specials and albums, and he continues to expand his creative work through both stand-up comedy and independent film projects. Most recently, he teamed with Nick Swardson and Doug Jones on Remain Calm , a horror-comedy short from writer-director Jake Lewis that is approaching 10M views on YouTube. Shore is repped by Curate and Vox. title: Russell Brand Trial: Prosecution Weaponizes “Amusement Park Of Orgasms” Quote Star Used In Wendy Williams Interview
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake AI Dubbing Pioneer Flawless Sells Technology In Deal That Raises Questions About Its Future Russell Brand’s Wife Says Star Was “Caring” Lover At Time Of Rape Allegations BAFTA Launches Review Over Concerns About Trustees Accepting Free Awards Guest Tickets View All October 30, 2026 8:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand Getty Russell Brand ‘s October 2017 appearance on The Wendy Williams Show has been used against him during his rape trial in London. The prosecution evoked the chat show in closing remarks on Friday at Southwark Crown Court, where Brand is on trial over three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one of attempted indecent assault. Deadline has been reporting daily on the trial from a live video feed of the courtroom. Riel Karmy-Jones, the prosecution barrister, told the jury: “Women were disposable … they didn’t matter to him [Brand]. They were the amusements, in what he described in a Wendy Williams interview as his ‘playground of orgasms.'” Related Stories News Russell Brand Rape Trial: Channel 4 Film Was Not "Magic Force" That Caused Accusers To "Recast" Memories, Court Hears In Closing Arguments Legal Russell Brand's Wife Says Star Was "Caring" Lover At Time Of Rape Allegations Karmy-Jones slightly misquoted Brand’s original words on Wendy Williams — which were that he thought “the world was like an amusement park made out of orgasms” when he was young — but she used it to illustrate her argument that the Despicable Me star was “rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever he wished.” It is not the first time the prosecution has referenced the Wendy Williams comment. Watch on Deadline In her final argument to the jury, Karmy-Jones alleged that Brand saw junior women in the workplace as a “disposable commodity.” Four of the six complainants worked in the television and radio industry at the time of their encounter with Brand. All have a lifelong right to anonymity, despite being identified in court and giving evidence during the trial. Karmy-Jones invited the jury to put themselves in the shoes of Complainant 6, a former Channel 4 employee, who alleged that Brand demanded a massage and “plonked his head, mouth, and nose into the area of her genitals” during a workplace incident in 2009. “How would you feel if someone in a position of power in your workplace did that to you?” she asked. Karmy-Jones began her closing remarks by reminding the jury that the six women behind the seven charges are “wholly unconnected” insofar as they “do not know each other and have never met.” She continued: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not taken part in documentaries, who have not made claims for compensation … There is no benefit to them.” Karmy-Jones said Russell Brand: In Plain Sight , the 2023 Channel 4 documentary, and reporting by The Times of London , had caused the women to come forward and tell stories about their encounters with Brand that had “haunted them for years.” In legal directions to the jury earlier on Friday, Mr Justice Bennathan, the judge presiding over the trial, said they must reach unanimous verdicts on each of the charges to convict Brand. He reminded jurors that the burden of proof is on the prosecution and that Brand is entitled to the benefit of the doubt. Bennathan expects the jury to begin verdict deliberations next Tuesday, November 3. The trial continues. title: Bobby Wright, ‘McHale’s Navy’ Actor, Singer and Son of Kitty Wells, Dies at 84
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 8:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bobby Wright on 'McHale's Navy' Courtesy Everett Collection Bobby Wright, the singer and son of country music legend Kitty Wells who played the radio operator Willy Moss on the popular ABC comedy McHale’s Navy , died Tuesday at his home in Madison, Tennessee, his family announced . He was 84. McHale’s Navy , starring Ernest Borgnine , Joe Flynn and Tim Conway , aired for four seasons (1962-66), and Wright appeared on all 138 episodes of the show that was set on the U.S. Navy boat PT-73 in the Pacific during World War II. He also appeared with the rest of the cast in the features McHale’s Navy (1964) and McHale’s Navy Joins the Air Force (1966). Related Stories Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist Movies Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies at 86 Wright recorded for Decca, ABC and United Artists Records from 1967-79 and had 21 singles on Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart, with the gentle “Here I Go Again” peaking at No. 13 in 1971. His other singles included “Lay Some Happiness on Me,” “Everybody Needs a Rainbow,” a cover of Terry Jacks’ “Seasons in the Sun,” “Lovin’ Someone on My Mind” and “I’m Turning You Loose.” One of three kids, John Robert Wright Jr. was born on March 30, 1942, in Charleston, West Virginia. His father was Johnnie Wright, who toured the South in an act called Johnnie & Jack, with Wells often performing with them. At age 8, he sang with his parents on the country music program Louisiana Hayride out of Shreveport and played guitar. He and his family moved to Nashville in 1958 when his folks became headliners at the Grand Ole Opry, and he graduated from Madison High School, where he played baseball, basketball and football. Wright came to Hollywood to audition for director Peter Tewksbury ( Father Knows Best , My Three Sons ) for a role on television as a Southern youngster who could play the guitar. The show didn’t move forward, but his screen test was seen by a producer on McHale’s Navy (he was billed as John Wright on the show). While the comedy was still in production, he gave music another try and worked with his mom on one of her 1965 albums. After McHale’s Navy ended, Wright played a robber on a 1966 episode of CBS’ Pistols ’n’ Petticoats , a short-lived Western that starred Anne Sheridan, and showed up in the 1974 film Catch the Black Sunshine , starring Ted Cassidy and Chris Robinson . Wright, who also played bass, trumpet and drums, appeared with his parents and sisters, Ruby and Carol Sue, on the syndicated Kitty Wells Johnnie Wright Family Show for years and toured with his parents until they retired from the road in 2007. Survivors include Carol Sue; his children, LeAnn and Kamela; his grandchildren, Austin, Cassidy, Shelby and Dalton; his great-grandchildren, Hayden, Pazlee, Remi, Fletcher and Axel; his nieces and nephews, Kitty, John Jr., David, Corrie and Stephanie; and his former wife, Brenda. Wells, a member of the Country Music Hall of Fame, was country’s first female superstar, racking up nearly three dozen Top 10 hits from 1952-65, including the No. 1 smash “It Wasn’t God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels.” THR

title: Canadian Rock Icon Bryan Adams Takes Aim at Trump, Says His Protest Song Gets Standing Ovations in Red States (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bryan Adams Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty Images He never says him by name — not in the songs and not in this interview. But there can be no mistaking who Bryan Adams is taking aim at in his recent musical output, a string of Canadian protest songs like “51st State” and his latest, the plaintive “Lake Ontario.” Adams has Donald Trump on the brain. Both of those songs appear on How’s It Goin’ , a Canadian concept album which drops Nov. 6 and features a dozen new tracks about Adams’ homeland. Related Stories News Russell Brand Treated Consent as "an Obstacle to Remove or Ignore," Prosecution Tells Jury in Rape Trial's Closing Arguments Movies Edinburgh Film Festival Toasts Bollywood With 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' Anniversary Event at 2028 Edition It’s the 17th studio album for the rocker — whose catalog of indestructible hits includes “Summer of ’69,” “Run to You” and “(Everything I Do) I Do It for You” — and easily his most politically pointed, having found a new muse in the deterioration of relations between his homeland and the United States. Since returning to the White House, Trump has placed punishing tariffs on Canadian goods, repeatedly threatened to make Canada the “51st state” and even ordered Lake Ontario renamed “Lake America” in U.S. federal records, inflaming tensions with the country’s longtime ally north of the 49th parallel. Adams, for one, has had enough. He checked in with The Hollywood Reporter from a tour stop in Las Vegas — he’s in the middle of a five-show run at the Wynn — to share where his head is at these days. It’s firmly grounded in the waning months of 2026, about as far as you can get from the summer of ’69. I’ve lived in L.A. for 25 years, but I grew up in Montreal. I’m still very much a proud Canadian. And I’ve got to say, listening to “Lake Ontario,” I got a little choked up. Wow, that’s super nice. Now wait till you hear the rest of the album. Half my family is still there, and it’s been a really rough couple of years. You put those dark feelings into these angry, beautiful words that really helped me process it a bit. I mean, it’s not even angry. It’s not? It’s not angry. It’s stating the facts. I’m just commenting on current affairs and feeling the temperature in the room, basically. Do you live in Canada? Yeah. So you might not be angry, but I know people there are very angry. No, I mean, listen, I might be angry, but I don’t think the songs are angry. I think there’s a lot of irony in there. And they’re heartfelt and funny. But it’s helping process what feels like a betrayal. You say it in the song : We’ve had so many years of peace and harmony, and it just takes “one dude” — and I’m wondering if “dude” was the original word you wanted to use — to fuck it all up. Yeah, “dude” was the original word. There are other expletives you could put in there, but I consider myself respectful as well, even under the circumstances. But the thing I really wanted to say is that if you have that much power, why would you not want to channel it for good? You could do so much good in the world with that much power, and it’s just not happening. So I think that’s the thing that perplexes me more than anything. Put Canada aside for one second and just look at the global situation. It’s baffling. How did the idea for the album come to you? Did it come out of this frustration? It started out that I was asked to write a song for a documentary on Canada, about Canada’s East Coast. When I write, I don’t just focus on one thing. I just start writing. Looking back on my notes, I noticed there were a few things I had that were potentially interesting. So I went down and finished that one, then I finished another one, and then I started getting into the current affairs thing. Before I knew it, I had three or four songs that seemed like part of a concept album. So I just kept going, and the whole album was written and recorded in three months. “51st State,” that was the first song on the album that was quite political. How did people react to it? We debuted that song in St. Louis on our tour this summer, and we weren’t sure how it was going to go down in America. But the first night we did it, standing ovation. Second night we did it, standing ovation. Got into Texas, into the red states, standing ovation. And I suddenly thought to myself, I’m not sure that the people in this country, in America — I’m in Las Vegas at the moment — I’m not sure everybody agrees with what’s going down. And that was the way of testing the temperature in the room, because if you play it live, you can see automatically what people think. We were getting just full-on cheers. Well, we’ll see in a few days what people really think, with the Nov. 3 election. It’s not worth predicting it at all. I’m just writing my truth. I want to bring up this viral thing that happened, and I return to it whenever I want to smile. It’s when that drunk guy came onstage during “Summer of ’69,” and you let it happen, and then you continued the song without missing a single beat. Not only is it funny, but it says something about you, I think. Which is? A lot of people would have been angry, would have been reactive, would have said, “Get this guy off the stage!” But you let the universe just happen. That’s me. That’s what I’m getting at. I feel that I saw the real you at that moment. Well, that’s nice. I think that’s actually very much what I am like. I let the universe do its thing. And when I saw that guy coming, I mean, I could have easily backed off, but I saw him coming and just thought, “Go for it, have a crack.” As he climbed onto the stage, he whacked his head. And I remember that moment, thinking, “He’s not going to make it all the way up here.” But he did. Oh dear. I’m glad somebody filmed it. Since we’re on the subject of “Summer of ’69.” I’m just curious, how much of those lyrics are true? Do you remember your summer of ’69? Did you really have a band with friends? The song is obviously bittersweet, and it’s a song of nostalgia, but it’s not about the year. Someone told me it’s about another kind of 69. I was like, “There’s no way.” Well, it’s just a metaphor. It’s about first love. It’s about first figuring out where you’re going, what you’re doing, and it’s about reflecting on how that summer went. But there’s no double entendre in there. Oh, of course there is. OK then! My friend is right. I was like, “Are you crazy? No, it’s about the summer of 1969!” Nowhere in the song do I say [1969]. Where did you get your first real six-string? My father. Well, I’m glad he got it for you. Same here. THR

title: Aerosmith Joined by Dave Grohl and Johnny Depp at Hollywood Bowl for First Show in Three Years, as GNR and Black Crowes Open With Tribute Sets: Concert Review
full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 8:27am PT Aerosmith Joined by Dave Grohl and Johnny Depp at Hollywood Bowl for First Show in Three Years, as GNR and Black Crowes Open With Tribute Sets: Concert Review By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Noah Kahan Announces ‘The Last of the Bugs World Tour’ in Stadiums for Spring and Summer 2027 1 day ago Donnie Iris, Pittsburgh’s Favorite Rocker, Who Scored Hits With the Jaggerz and as a Solo Artist, Dies at 83 3 days ago Taylor Swift, Inducted Into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, Says ‘There Is No Music Community Like This Music Community. I Know, I Checked All the Communities’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation With Aerosmith , fans might not want to miss a thing, but they most especially did not want to miss — if at all possible — the band’s two all-star-guest-augmented shows at the Hollywood Bowl this week, the first of which was Thursday night. These two outings are the group’s first shows since they had to cut their farewell tour abruptly short a little over three years ago. Could they also be the last? No one has said anything official about this representing an actual finale for Aerosmith, and so many fans have figured that they may have further shows in them after this, perhaps going out at some point in the future with a hometown gig in Boston, in that line of prospective thinking. And yet, there was the show’s host, Bill Burr, at the very top of the evening, captured on video for all the world to hear declaring that these were “the final two shows in Aerosmith’s history.” The casual way in which he dropped that bombshell while introducing show-opener Warren Hayne made it clear he was speaking out of turn. But was Burr letting a real cat out of the bag? (Or, considering that he did a lengthy comic monologue about getting a DUI as a youth on his way home from an Aerosmith show, had he just dipped back into the sauce backstage for old time’s sake?) If these two shows should be the end of the line — rather than just being put together for the sake of filming for a TV special or documentary, as seemed to be happening — it would be a fairly proud way to go out, as the band sounded in completely top form during a short-ish but spectacular 45-minute set that rounded out the nearly four-hour evening. In particular, Steven Tyler gave no evidence of the vocal injury that halted the abortive 2023 tour. Not just back in the saddle — Tyler and Joe Perry, Tom Hamilton and Brad Whitford did not sound or act like cowpokes who had any immediate intention of re-vacating their seats upon the horse they rode in on. (L-R) Steven Tyler and Joey Kramer of Aerosmith perform onstage during California, Dream On: Aerosmith & Friends – Night 1 at the Hollywood Bowl on October 29, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation) Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation The asterisk on all that was the participation of original drummer Joey Kramer, who had had to take a break from the band due to health issues even prior to the ’23 interruption, but had made it clear he didn’t want to be done. For the first five numbers of Aerosmith’s six-song climactic set Thursday, the drummer on duty was Dave Grohl , slamming it home as if he were slugger Shohei Ohtani in his pre-midseason prime. So the question of “what about Joey?” was begged when, toward the end, Tyler said, “Before we say goodnight, I just want to say what a ride it’s been with my brothers — Joe, Tom, Brad and Joey,. Fifty-five fucking years, and we’re the same fucking band that started fifty-five and a half years ago.” (You’ve got to love a guy who’s so proud of his permanent record that he remembers to throw the “and a half” in there.) And there. suddenly, was Kramer, at center stage, sharing a hug with the frontman. He then retreated to the second drum kit that had been sitting out, promissorily, with the initials “JK” on it. Grohl gave up his position on the main kit and left the stage so that it could be taken over by John Douglas, the drum tech who had come to fill in previously for Kramer. As the two men drummed side-by-side on the final number, it seemed evident that Kramer was capable of laying down a good beat but probably not capable of doing the heavy lifting at this point in time. And so the way that it was handled seemed like a good, bittersweet compromise, in allowing the co-founder to come out and collect his flowers at the close as a still-working performer. No one from the general public who’d bought a ticket had too much idea what to expect out of Aerosmith for these two shows. So some might have thought the 45 minutes were too brief, although a look at the all-star lineup (some of whom will be repeating Sunday night, and some of whom will rotate out) made it clear to anyone attentive that this would not be a full career-summation kind of show. There were no sentimental musings, beyond Tyler’s aforementioned 55-and-a-half remarks. At the end of “Walk This Way,” without any farewells being offered, fireworks started going off over the Bowl’s shell, and it was unclear whether they’d be coming back for more after the sparklers went out or not. They did not, which made things feel a bit anticlimactic. Presumably, they’ll end night 2 with a slight bit more speechifying, whether or not they’re in the mood for clarifying future prospects or an end to all that. Anyway, aside from the odd finish, what the Bowl audience got in the broader sense was far from an anticlimax in the overall scheme of things. They wanted to see Aerosmith performing with the vigor of a mirage reassembling before their eyes, or as if there were four portraits of Dorian Gray being held in storage back in the green room. Against the odds of layoffs and advancing time, that’s exactly what they got. Long scarves tied to the mic stand and blowing in the wind? Check. Even longer hair on Tyler and Perry, also blowing in those hurricane-level breezes, with the singer festooned in a beautiful open blouse? Check. The band in crunchy precision, and the singer howling like he’d never taken a hiatus from dreaming on? Double-check. Whatever injury went down with Tyler’s larynx, it was apparently reversible, and he seems to have the kind of chops that naturally age well… which no one would take for granted after hearing some bumpy moments from some of the opening attractions. It was all you could have hoped for from the Aerosmith of 2026, and maybe even a little better than that. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!' ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With (L-R) Tom Hamilton, Steven Tyler and Joe Perry of Aerosmith perform onstage during California, Dream On: Aerosmith & Friends – Night 1 at the Hollywood Bowl on October 29, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation) Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation Grohl was not the only guest musician to sit in with Aerosmith, as Perry brought out his Hollywood Vampires bandmate, “Johnny fucking Depp,” to play on the penultimate number, “Train Kept A-Rollin’.” Lest any cynics imagine the actor did not have his instrument plugged in for his rhythm playing, Perry actually tossed Depp a spot to take half of his guitar solo, which he pulled off with fleeting aplomb. But the highlight might have occurred one song before that, with “Dream On,” which is a predictable choice for a standout, but when something that time-tested works, you don’t have to go looking for an underdog pick just for the sake of it. Tyler began the anthem accompanying himself on grand piano (while the audio from an interlude video was still playing) and eventually revealed that there was a small staircase behind the gleaming instrument, as there he was on top of it, preening and posing for the post-high-note outro like only someone of his greatest (?) generation can get away with. We love our Geese, and their modern-day modesty, but we may still love Tyler as a strutting, raunchy swan a little bit more. The two acts on the bill that got full mini-sets prior to Aerosmith’s appearance were the Black Crowes and Guns N’ Roses, each of whom devoted either most or all of their time on stage to covering the headliner. The BC guys were all about the Aerosmith, capably holding down the Joe Perry Project song “Let the Music Do the Talking” as their opener, followed by “Write Me a Letter,” “Combination,” “No More No More” and, finally, “Chip Away the Stone.” GNR did also did a five-song set, with three of those five being Aerosmith covers — “Nobody’s Fault,” “Seasons of Wither” and a delectable “Last Child” — before adding value for the audience with “Sweet Child of Mine” and “Welcome to the Jungle.” Slash was on form, and Axl Rose was game, though better in his lower range; in his upper, he sounded… well, different… sort of more like a choirboy falsetto, as heard here, than the raspier instrument we remember. Settling into and enjoying that difference may take more acclimation than we all had time for in such a quick appearance. Most everyone else on the bill got two numbers. With country superstar Eric Church, you’d have to count it as a split decision. “Rag Doll” was a lot of fun, given a very rootsy treatment. But “I Don’t Want to Miss a Thing” was, well, a miss, with the singer trying a little too strenuously to match Tyler’s intensity, while spending the entire number notably staring downward through his shades at the words on a monitor. It’s unclear whether he will also be on the bill for night 2, but he could use a do-over on that one; with a little more prep, it might yet be within his reach. Church was working with a house band that included Don Was, Kenny Aronoff, Andrew Watt and other famous names, as were those that preceded him — Heart’s Wilson sisters, Sammy Hagar, Billy Idol with Steve Stevens, Warren Haynes, and Sully of Godsmack. Chances are that most of those performers will not be returning for the second Bowl show, since a lot of the advertised acts have yet to appear, like Run-DMC, Tom Morello, Marcus King, Jerry Cantrell and Train’s Pat Monahan. Unless, that is, they are planning to move the start time for Sunday up even further than they did for Thursday; ticketholders for this first show got a warning through their apps in the afternoon that the very action-packed bill would be kicking off at 6:45 instead of 7. The two shows are being produced by by 724 Management and Blackbird Presents, with the involvement of the latter company being a sure sign that a doc or special is in store, pretty much confirmed by the presence of a flying camera on wires swooping back and forth above the venue’s box seats. The world will likely get a chance to see it, then, in some form. But only time — or maybe some additional remarks from the stage on Sunday? — will tell whether there might be still additional chances to see the band in the flesh down the road. title: Matthew Weiner Out as Showrunner of Eddie Murphy Peacock Series After Clash With Producers
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 30, 2026 8:23am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matthew Weiner ANTHONY HARVEY/AFP/Getty Images Matthew Weiner has exited Eddie Murphy ‘s Peacock series The Chairman following a clash with producers, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. Murphy is among the producers. Weiner ( Mad Men ) was the project’s showrunner. The reason given for his departure was “creative differences.” A new showrunning team is already in place, we’re told, and will be announced soon. The writers room has been shuttered for two weeks amid the transition. THR reached out to Weiner for comment did not immediately respond back. Related Stories TV Alexander Brothers Case Is a "Microcosm for a Lot of Questions about Sexual Assault," Says Doc Director Business Peacock's Hot Streak: Two Quarters of Profit After Years Of Losses Variety first reported the news of Weiner’s exit. The Chairman is being produced by Universal Television and David Glasser’s ( Yellowstone ) 101 Studios, which has a first-look film and television deal at NBCUniversal. The show also stands out as the first project from Chris McCarthy under his overall deal with NBCU. (McCarthy followed his buddy Taylor Sheridan over from Paramount.) The plot of The Chairman remains under wraps . The Chairman will be Murphy’s first TV series regular role since NBC’s Saturday Night Live , which launched his comedy career. He served as a cast member on the sketch comedy series for four seasons from 1980 to 1984. Murphy is often credited with having saved the struggling SNL — he even hosted it once as a cast member when movie star Nick Nolte fell sick. (And then twice more as planned.) Murphy later went on to star in dozens of films, including the Beverly Hills Cop franchise, 1996’s The Nutty Professor , 1998’s Doctor Dolittle , 2003’s The Haunted Mansion , 2003’s Daddy Day Care , 2008’s Meet Dave and 2023’s You People . Murphy’s also voiced multiple characters, such as Donkey in the Shrek franchise and Thurgoode Orenthal Stubbs in The PJs . In 2007, he was nominated for an Academy Award for best supporting actor for Dreamgirls . Weiner has won nine Emmy awards, mostly for his iconic AMC series Mad Men . He was also a writer and executive producer on The Sopranos . Other credits include The Romanoffs , Becker and Are You Here . In 2017, Kater Gordon, an Emmy-winning writer for Mad Men , accused Weiner of sexual harassment . Gordon said that while working late one night, Weiner told her she owed it to him to let him see her naked. She was let go from the series a year later. Weiner has repeatedly denied Gordon’s allegations, telling the New York Times in October 2018, “I have reasons I don’t believe that I said it, if that makes sense, but I really don’t remember saying it.” For its part, 101 Studios has gone through numerous showrunner shuffles itself, mostly on Sheridan shows. title: ‘Blindspot Berlin,’ a Beta Film TIFF Standout With ‘All Quiet’ Star Albrecht Schuch, Seals Deal for Spain with Filmin (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 8:21am PT ‘Blindspot Berlin,’ a Beta Film TIFF Standout With ‘All Quiet’ Star Albrecht Schuch, Seals Deal for Spain with Filmin (EXCLUSIVE) The deal for the counter-terror police task force thriller comes ahead of the series’ Spanish premiere at the South International Series Festival in Cádiz By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest South International Series Festival: ‘American Hostage,’ Ronan Bennett, Great European Series and Andalusia’s TV Build 3 days ago Lula’s Election Win: How Fan Accounts for Taylor Swift, Billie Eilish and More Helped Him to a Historic Victory and Defeat for Trump 4 days ago ‘Killing a Bear,’ From Movistar Plus and Arte France: a Real-Event Inspired Murder-Mystery Whose Victim Is a Pyrenean Brown Bear 7 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Blindspot Berlin (Courtesy of Neuesuper/Hubert Mican) “ Blindspot Berlin ,” a buzzy counter-terror police unit thriller led by “All Quiet on the Western Front” star Albrecht Schuch has been licensed by Beta Film to Spain’s upscale SVOD platform Filmin. Backed by Germany’s ARD, Europe’s biggest public broadcaster as well as rbb, NDR, and HR, “Blindspot Berlin’s” Spanish deal was announced Friday on the eve of the six-part series screening in main competition at Cadiz’s South International Series Festival. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’ ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!' The news comes as “Blindspot Berlin” launches Oct. 30 on ARD’s streaming service, with linear broadcasts on Nov. 1 and Nov. 6. The series will be made available on Filmin in early 2027. A true crime thriller, the heavily researched “Blindspot Berlin” charts German police efforts to prevent Berlin’s Dec. 19 2016 Christmas market terror attack which killed 13 and injured dozens. A standout world premiere at TIFF Primetime, where it was one of only two European series to make its cut, it turns on Detective Lieutenant Frank Laudlin (Schuch) and Iraq-born rookie police officer Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla, “Elaha”), based out of Düsseldorf State’s Criminal Police H.Q., who race at first to dismantle ISIS recruiting young Germans. Planting an informant, Murat Cem (Tamer Tıraşoğlu, “Unfamiliar,” “Manta Manta”), their concern soon turns, however, to a threatened terror outrage on German soil, inspired by 2015’s Paris attacks. Yet as Laudlin’s task force closes in on a key suspect, its efforts are undermined by the very German institutions meant to support them. Schuch is well known for his performances in “All Quiet on the Western Front,” “Bad Banks,” “Berlin Alexanderplatz” and “System Crasher.” Layla was selected this year as one of this year’s German Films Face to Face talents. The ensemble cast also includes Wael Alkhatib (“Sun and Concrete”), Jeanne Goursaud , star of “Exterritorial” and “Barbarians”), Bernd Hölscher (“The Captain,”) and Sina Martens (“From Hilde, with Love”). Tense from the get-go thriller, fuelled by an atmospheric electronic score and co-created, co-written and directed by David Nawrath (“Your Honor,” “Atlas”), “Blindspot Berlin” is produced by Neuesuper (“8 Days”), one of Germany’s most ambitious production houses. Much of the series is set in claustrophobic corridors, backrooms and basements, endowing it with the sense of a labyrinth that its anti-terror agents have to navigate. It also adopts the multiple POVs of Laudlin, Al-Husseini and Cem, meaning viewers are often one step ahead of Maudlin and certainly German top-flight security officials who deam their prime suspect an ”improbable threat” and pull his monitoring. “Blindspot Berlin” records all the decisions made before the tragic event and the “systemic failures and human errors that led to this catastrophe,” Nawrath told Variety . “So many things went wrong. There were so many crazy situations we didn’t have time to show them,” added co-writer David Marian. “From the moment we watched the first episodes, we had no hesitation in acquiring the series for Filmin. It is an outstanding example of how to craft a thriller based on true events while remaining entirely faithful to the real story, said Jaume Ripoll, co-founder and CCO of Filmin. He added: “Its technical excellence, exceptional performances, and direction that revives the very best of the European thriller tradition make ‘Blindspot Berlin’ one of Filmin’s flagship series for the first quarter of 2027.” “‘Blindspot Berlin’ turns a chapter of recent German history into a gripping, character-driven thriller with universal appeal. Its combination of true-crime urgency, outstanding performances, and a story about the consequences of institutional failure makes it a powerful proposition for international audiences,” said Christian Gockel, Beta Film EVP international operations Spain and Portugal. “Filmin recognized that potential. We are proud that ‘Blindspot Berlin’ already premiered at TIFF and Hamburg, and will now celebrate its Spanish premiere at the South International Series Festival in Cádiz. We are confident that the series will continue to engage audiences around the world,” Glockel continued. Beta Film is a producer/distributor of many of the continent’s biggest titles such as “Babylon Berlin,” “Gomorrah,” “Borgia,” “Sisi” and evergreen “Rex.” Founded in 2007, Filmin has grown to one of the highest-profile Spanish SVOD services, acquiring select upscale series and independent and auteur films, as it has begun to produce its own original series, such as Serielizados-selected “Segunda Temporada” as well as acquiring the distribution business of top Spanish arthouse/crossover producer-distributor Elastica Films. ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians’ Debuts New Season 3 Footage at Lucca Comics as Stars and Creator Tease the Show’s ‘First Real Bad Guy’ ‘Monarch: Legacy of Monsters’ Eyes Season 3 Renewal at Apple TV With New Writers, Showrunner 25 In-the-Know Gifts for Women: Mahjong Boards, ACOTAR Merch, Nathan Fielder Lingerie and More Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival Annecy Winner ‘The Violinist’ Found Its Italian Co-Producers at Tokyo Market, Director Ervin Han Tells Anime Co-Production Panel David Bowie’s Immersive ‘Stage’ Concert Experience: Director Brett Morgen on the Show, the Artist and the Archive (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

title: Terry Sanders Wraps Documentary ‘On Rescuing Democracy And The Rule Of Law’
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart ‘Talk To Me’ Backer Head Gear Opens U.S. Arm With Ambitious Indie Investment Plan Sphere Media & Paul Barbeau Team Up To Bring TV Drama To Quebec Maxine Peake Boards Short Film ‘The Secret Assistants’ Exploring Power Imbalances In The Movie Business View All October 30, 2026 8:17am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Terry Sanders doc ‘On Rescuing Democracy And The Rule Of Law’ American Film Foundation EXCLUSIVE: Terry Sanders has finished his latest project On Rescuing Democracy and the Rule of Law . Two-time Oscar winner Sanders writes and directs the documentary. It explores the challenges and threats that established democracies, including the U.S., are facing and tells the story of the people who became involved with the Central and East European Law Initiative (CEELI) after the fall of the Berlin Wall. The doc tells the story of how more than 5,000 American lawyers, judges and legal experts became involved with CEELI, which was a pro bono initiative that provided technical legal assistance to former Soviet Bloc countries. Its work included helping to rewrite the constitutions of these countries, reform court systems, and adopt democratic rule of law principles. Related Stories News HBO's Harry Potter Casts Its Ghosts, Sorting Hat & Fat Lady On Halloween Eve News Forest Whitaker Joins Rachid Bouchareb's 'Boomerang Atomic' As EP Ahead Of DOC NYC Screening Former U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has said: “In my judgment, CEELI is the most effective voluntary legal assistance initiative in history.” Watch on Deadline Veteran filmmaker Sanders is co-head of the American Film Foundation, which produced On Rescuing Democracy and the Rule of Law . His earlier work includes producing Oscar-winning short A Time Out of War and co-producing Maya Lin: A Strong Clear Vision , which won the Best Documentary Feature Oscar. The team behind the new film said it will document how populist surges have softened some countries’ resolve to protect established democratic rule of law, and how the U.S. experienced a violent assault on the Capitol on January 6, 2021. Sanders explained to Deadline his the 33-minute doc is in three parts. It starts at the end of WWII and the Cold War, before taking in the fall of the Berlin Wall and rise of democracy in former Soviet Bloc countries. It goes on to take in events including January 6, before looking at the rise of authoritarianism and concluding with segments on the situation today and where we head next. On Rescuing Democracy and the Rule of Law has contributions from Homer Moyer, co-founder of CEELI, Mark Ellis, Executive Director of the International Bar Association, Betsy Andersen, former Executive Director of the World Justice Project as well as Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O’Connor and historian Corey Brettschneider. title: Russell Brand Treated Consent as “an Obstacle to Remove or Ignore,” Prosecution Tells Jury in Rape Trial’s Closing Arguments
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 8:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Oct. 30, 2026. Courtesy of Getty The prosecution has made its closing arguments in Russell Brand ‘s highly publicized rape and sexual assault trial in London, saying his defense is “a lot of half-truths, but spun into lies.” The jury, made up of eight men and four women, will now deliberate. The judge will only accept a unanimous verdict on each count. As The Hollywood Reporter has covered in detail, the presenter and comedian (also star of St Trinian’s and Forgetting Sarah Marshall ) is accused of three counts of rape and three charges of sexual assault. He was initially accused of indecent assault, which was reduced to a count of attempted indecent assault by the judge on Tuesday. Six women allege offenses dating from 1999 to 2009, and Brand denies the allegations vehemently. Related Stories Movies Edinburgh Film Festival Toasts Bollywood With 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' Anniversary Event at 2028 Edition Movies From 'Sh*t Happens' to an Erotic Photographer Being Confronted by His Daughter: Offbeat Films at Tallinn London’s Southwark Crown Court has heard from the complainants, one of whom says she was raped by Brand in a Bournemouth hotel room after the Labour Party conference in 1999. Another alleges Brand pulled her into a nearby toilet and orally raped her at a bar in Soho in 2004 and a separate accuser says she was anally raped by the star at his Hampstead home in 2009, after the two had consensual vaginal sex. Brand is also said to have attempted to drag an MTV colleague into a bathroom at work in 2001, and exposed himself while traveling with a complainant in a car, telling her to “suck it.” Over the last three weeks, the jury has watched police interviews with all of the complainants, whose identities have been kept anonymous during the trial. Their testimonies have been cross-examined, witnesses — including Brand’s former personal assistant, Helen Berger — have been called to the stand, and Brand himself gave evidence just this week. He revealed he hadn’t persuaded anyone to testify on his behalf, but his wife, Laura, did take the stand on Thursday and told the room that Brand is a “caring and kind, wonderful father” to their three children. The defendant himself maintained : “I know what ‘no’ means… Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary and in many ways more important than sex itself.” Lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told the jury in her closing argument on Friday that these six women do not know each other. None of them “sought the limelight” or “any kind of publicity,” she said. “None of these women has anything to gain — except perhaps some closure.” She urged the jury: “Listen to their accounts, how many said he was nice, then there was a personality change, a pivot.” She said these women have told the court: “[Brand] didn’t listen when I said no, he didn’t listen, he didn’t care… In the rape cases, he just kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim and ejaculated.” All of the accusers have since moved on with their lives, but the trial has forced them to “relive what has happened to them” and describe intimate details to the court, Karmy-Jones also said. They are not “jealous women spurned,” as one complainant was made out to seem, she continued, and it doesn’t matter that the complainants “can’t remember” what they wore. She also said Brand seemed to “remember lots now” despite initially not being able to recollect many of the encounters in his police interviews. Brand’s defense is “a lot of half-truths, but spun into lies,” said Karmy-Jones. At this moment, per Sky News coverage , proceedings were briefly interrupted by the snoring of a member of the public who had fallen asleep in the gallery. Karmy-Jones also said that Channel 4’s Dispatches , a documentary built from allegations against Brand that kickstarted the 2023 police investigation, was not a “magic force” that caused the women to “recast” memories of “happy consensual fun.” Instead, these women “have realized they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth.” Karmy-Jones asked the jury to sit in silence for 20 seconds — the same length of time one woman alleges her encounter with Brand, as he attempted to pull her into the toilet, lasted. The prosecution also described Brand’s wife as “undoubtedly lovely” but said Laura Brand was not in touch with the defendant at the time the alleged encounters took place. Karmy-Jones quoted one of Brand’s earlier statements: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself,” before asking the jury: Does that ring true?” She pulled a quote from Brand’s 2007 autobiography My Booky Wook . He wrote: “Now if I want something — whether it’s a job or a woman — I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that’s in the way, until I possess the object of my desire.” Karmy-Jones said consent was maybe “just an obstacle to be removed, or perhaps to ignore,” for Brand. Brand had a “tendency” to “swiftly make things sexual,” said Karmy-Jones, wrapping up. Court has ended for the week. The defense’s closing arguments will take place on Monday. THR

title: Dominic Cooke to Direct ‘John Daniel,’ Real-Life Story of Woman’s Friendship With Baby Gorilla in Post-WWI England, as Cornerstone Boards Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 8:00am PT Dominic Cooke to Direct ‘John Daniel,’ Real-Life Story of Woman’s Friendship With Baby Gorilla in Post-WWI England, as Cornerstone Boards Sales (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Dominic Cooke to Direct ‘John Daniel,’ Real-Life Story of Woman’s Friendship With Baby Gorilla in Post-WWI England, as Cornerstone Boards Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 31 minutes ago Tahmima Anam’s New Novel ‘Good Books’ Being Adapted for TV With Pacesetter, Kudos and ‘Emily in Paris’ Writer (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Disney+ Strikes Landmark Content Deal With U.K.’s Channel 4 That Streamer Says Is Among Its ‘Most Significant’ Globally 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Supplied Acclaimed British theater director Dominic Cooke , behind the recent stage spin-off “Game of Thrones: The Mad King,” is to helm his first film since 2020’s Benedict Cumberbatch-starring spy thriller “The Courier.” “John Daniel,” which has been acquired for worldwide sales by Cornerstone ahead of the American Film Market, is based on the extraordinary true story of an unlikely friendship between a fiercely independent Englishwoman and a baby gorilla in the aftermath of WWI. With a screenplay written by Alexi Kaye Campbell (“Woman in Gold”), the film is inspired by original home movie footage and photographs recorded by locals in Uley, Gloucestershire between 1918-22. According to the filmmakers, motion capture and VFX will be used to “deliver a photoreal performance” of the gorilla, with visual effects by Axio World, led by Loris Mantello (“Avengers: Infinity War,” “Prehistoric Planet,” “The Lion King”) and Maoris Creantor (“The Lion King,” “Fast & Furious 9,” “The Matrix Resurrections”). Set in 1918 in the Cotwolds village of Uley, still raw from the losses of WWII, “John Daniel” follows Alyce Cunningham, who has built a solitary life behind a wall of wit and stoicism. As per the synopsis, that changes when her reckless nephew impulsively rescues a baby gorilla from the window of a London department store and, ignoring her protests, leaves her no option but to take him in. Mischievous and endlessly curious, John Daniel, as she reluctantly names him, slowly wins her over, and as he becomes part of village life, from the school classroom to the village pub, he brings joy back to the grieving community. When fear and suspicion threaten to drive him out, Alyce must decide how far she will go to protect the animal who has opened her heart. “The moment I read this beautiful script by Alexi, I knew I wanted to be part of it,” said Gray. “It’s an extraordinary true story about a gorilla, but at its heart it’s a story of love, hope and human connection in the aftermath of war. At a time when the world can feel increasingly divided, this film reminds us of our capacity to heal, unite and find compassion again.” Added Cooke: “I am delighted to be attached to direct John Daniel – a beautiful, funny and profound story. Alexi’s script gets to the heart of the strange, necessary bonds between humans and animals. It shows how we sometimes need to surrender control in order to feel fully alive. I couldn’t be happier to be working with such committed and driven producers as Debbie Gray and the team at Cornerstone to bring this moving and hopeful true story to life.” “John Daniel” marks the third feature from Cooke following “The Courier” and his 2017 directorial debut “On Chesil Beach,” based on Ian McEwan’s Booker Prize-nominated novella and starring Saoirse Ronan and Billy Howle. Cooke is represented by UTA and Casarotto Ramsay & Associates. title: Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’
full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 7:58am PT Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ 32 minutes ago Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival 52 minutes ago Sharjah Film Festival Partners With UAE’s Media Authority in Push to Assist Emerging Filmmakers 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "The Mangrove House" (Courtesy of Faradees) Two Emirati filmmakers are bringing distinctly local stories to the 13th edition of the Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth, with Khalid Al Mahmood ’s musical “The Mangrove House” and Abdulrahman Al Madani ’s family drama “Oug,” the only Emirati films in competition. Both filmmakers have longstanding ties to SIFF. “The Mangrove House,” which world premiered as the festival’s opening film, was pitched at SIFF’s inaugural Film Pitching Session last year as Al Mahmood was seeking post-production support. FANN – Media Discovery Platform, SIFF’s parent organization, subsequently came aboard to back the film. For Al Madani, “Oug” marks the third film he has screened at the festival, following “Nagafa,” which played at SIFF in 2015, and “Laymoon” in 2019. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!' “Oug” Courtesy of Abdulrahman Al Madani Their return comes as Emirati filmmakers see renewed momentum around a local industry that has weathered significant ups and downs over the past two decades. Al Mahmood, who made his first film while a university student in the U.S. in 1999, recalls returning to a UAE where filmmaking was virtually nonexistent, just as an early community of filmmakers was beginning to take shape. Annual screenings of locally made films, which later took shape as the Emirates Film Competition, became “a school where we came together and critiqued our films,” he explains. “More and more festivals popped up,” including the Dubai Intl. Film Festival and Abu Dhabi Film Festival. Al Madani entered the industry shortly before much of that festival ecosystem disappeared and remembers the “privilege” of having an abundance of platforms before “the plug was pulled, and then we didn’t know where to go next.” Abu Dhabi Film Festival remains defunct, while Dubai, which held its last edition in 2017, is set to return in December 2027. Khalid Al Mahmood, Abdulrahman Al Madani Courtesy of Essie Assibu, Muhammad Reda The loss pushed Al Madani and many Emirati filmmakers of his generation beyond the UAE. In the decade that followed, he made shorts that traveled internationally, an experience he describes as a “wake-up call” that taught him not to solely rely on platforms at home. Institutional support across the emirates is now growing. “Oug” received a grant from the UAE Ministry of Culture, a significant shift from a period Al Madani describes as having virtually “zero support.” “We have a long way to go, but I think this is a good start,” he acknowledges. “People feel like they can go and apply somewhere [local] to get funding.” For Al Mahmood, however, much of the UAE’s film infrastructure remains geared toward attracting international productions rather than sustaining local filmmakers. “What’s missing to me is just the infrastructure to be able to make films in the country,” he argues. Distribution presents another challenge. This year Al Madani launched Meylas Aflam, a screening initiative aimed at giving Emirati shorts a life beyond their initial festival runs. “We screen our film once, then what?” he asks. Meylas Aflam has held four sold-out screenings this year, with local audiences staying for discussions that have run as long as an hour. The response challenges what Al Madani calls a “misconception that our audience is not prepared for our stories.” His films on YouTube have drawn millions of views, he adds, with viewers responding to stories from their own environment “told truthfully, and without sugarcoating.” ‘The Mangrove House’ Al Mahmood’s “The Mangrove House” is a musical about two deaf brothers and their sister trying to raise money for a competition. The project originated with Emirati writer and editor Ayesha Alameri, whose brother is deaf and whose family uses sign language at home. Al Mahmood admits that when Alameri first brought him the screenplay, he expected the kind of story about living with a disability he had seen before. “Usually the stories are all sad, and it’s going to be a sob story,” he recalls. Instead, what appealed to him was precisely what the screenplay avoided. “There’s no pity. I didn’t feel like they were anything less than any other character.” That approach grew out of Alameri’s own conversations with her brother. When the two watched films and videos featuring deaf characters, she remembers him asking why their stories “always have to be sad.” Alameri’s original screenplay ran 23 pages, leaving Al Mahmood with a story he felt was too long to produce affordably as a short but not developed enough for a feature. He concentrated the film around one section of the script and then proposed another departure from its original form, asking, “Why not? Let’s do a musical.” That decision also gave Al Mahmood an opportunity to root the film more firmly in the UAE, weaving local instruments, clothing and even songs playing with the names of different fish into the story. “I always felt like I need to introduce something from this part of the world, something that’s rooted here,” he explains. “If it’s not the landscape, it’s the clothing, something.” ‘Oug’ Al Madani draws “Oug” from experiences around him. The title translates as “the defect,” referring to the blame directed at women whose marriages have yet to produce children. The idea grew out of conversations with married women he knew who faced intrusive questions about when they would have children, including a relative who undertook diets, exercise and other measures. “I was telling her, what about your husband? Does he have to do anything?” Al Madani recalls. “So this question stuck.” Set largely during a shopping trip to IKEA, the film follows a couple (Sarra’a Abdulaziz, Yaser Al Neyadi) as those pressures surface in a confrontation with the husband’s mother (Huda Al Ghanem). “I wanted it to be completely in a public setting,” Al Madani explains. “They are fighting, but they have to remain composed also. So I felt like it makes it much stronger.” He also resisted reducing the mother-in-law to a straightforward villain, instead portraying a family in which each character is responding to different expectations. That includes the husband, whose vulnerability culminates in an emotional breakdown. When Al Madani filmed the scene, he recalls crew members reacting to the sight of an Emirati man in kandura and ghutra, traditional clothing, crying onscreen. “I didn’t realize I was doing a thing,” he admits. “I was just staying true to the story.” The film’s international run has produced other unexpected reactions. At Denmark’s Odense Film Festival, where “Oug” premiered last year, Al Madani remembers audience members expressing surprise that its hijab-wearing women were the dominant personalities rather than passive figures. “I was not trying to break stereotypes,” he stresses. “I’m just portraying the truth of my environment, and somehow that broke so many stereotypes.” For both filmmakers, the next challenge is moving beyond shorts. Al Mahmood has an early-stage feature project he describes only as “very artistic,” while Al Madani has spent the past year developing a feature screenplay and identifies funding as the principal obstacle to making that transition. “This is my seventh short film. So I am ready,” Al Madani says. “My next project has to be a feature.” He argues that he is hardly alone. “There’s a community of filmmakers who have done countless short films,” he adds, “and we need to move on to the next step.” Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ Patrick Stewart Dies: Marvel, Kevin Feige Praise ‘X-Men’ Icon For Bringing ‘Charles Xavier to Life With Grace, Intelligence and Humanity’ Mexico City Grand Prix 2026: Here’s Where to Watch F1 Online for Free How ‘Up Again’ Director Captured the Rise of a Teenage Figure Skating Champion: ‘The Technical Conditions Were Extremely Challenging’ Taylor Sheridan’s ‘The Last Cowboy’ Sets Season 7 Premiere Date on CMT (EXCLUSIVE) Mohammad Rasoulof, Shahrbanoo Sadat Push Back on Idea of Separate Oscar Category for Exiled Filmmakers as Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund Hits Tokyo Loading comments...

title: Jaalen Best Wanted to Be a Pro Athlete. Now He’s Playing ‘The Greatest’ Boxer Onscreen
full_text: × Skip to main content Jaalen Best Photograph by Juan Veloz This story might sound familiar: a rising student discovering who he is as he juggles his love for both the court and the stage. However, this isn’t High School Musical . It’s the beginning of Jaalen Best’s trek to Hollywood, which started his junior year at East Carolina University in 2019 and led him to his breakout role, portraying legendary boxer Muhammad Ali . After stumbling into an intro to acting class, the 28-year-old quickly caught the professor’s attention. “She would tell me how great I was at improv and how I had a face for television and I should consider moving out to a bigger city or state and pursuing acting,” Best recalls. Related Stories Movies 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' Extends Theatrical Run as Amazon MGM Says Movie "Delivered Against Our Goals" (Exclusive) Movies Sacha Baron Cohen's 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' to Stream on Prime Video Days After Brief Theatrical Stint But he wasn’t ready to hear that yet. “I’m like, ‘I’m a basketball player. This ain’t happening.'” Best later got another acting push from his then-girlfriend, who convinced him to audition for his hometown production of Pocahontas in Clinton, North Carolina. Though skeptical at first, he decided to give it a real shot, landing the role of Pocahontas’ father, Chief Powhatan. “I would wake up early at 5 a.m., and I would do basketball practice for the first three hours of my day, finish classes, and then I would drive an hour and a half to my hometown and do two-hour rehearsal,” he says. Despite the chaotic schedule, Best eventually came to a realization while on stage: “I was having more fun than basketball.” While recounting this period of his life with The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom earlier in October, Best playfully acknowledges the similarities to the beloved Zac Efron-led Disney movie, with one exception: “I wasn’t the star player. I was riding the bench and just getting my opportunity,” he quips. Much like how Troy Bolton moved away to college to pursue his dreams, Best made the decision to move to Los Angeles post-college to follow his own. Jaalen Best in The Greatest . Prime Video The first few years in Tinseltown proved challenging, as Best was one of thousands who came to the city with the same goals. But after years of background work, occasional guest roles and finding new talent representation, he finally got the audition he had been longing for in 2023. “There were maybe seven or eight auditions,” he recalls, referring to the months-long audition process for the role of Muhammad Ali in Prime Video ‘s The Greatest , which premieres Nov. 4. “It also was during the [actors] strike as well, so a lot of it was completely delayed and being pushed back.” As months drew by between auditions and no confirmed offers, Best sought other roles. He later got offered a six-month contract with Days of Our Lives , but admits he was still holding out hope for The Greatest . That’s when his team flagged producers on the biopic of his pending soap opera booking and “instantly they’re like, ‘OK, we’re sending him to L.A. to do a network test,'” the actor recalls. A day after the test, as he headed back to the airport, Best receives a call that The Greatest creator Ben Watkins wants to meet at his office. “I walk in and I shake his hand, and he’s just telling me, ‘Hey, there’s a couple of executives that don’t think you can hold up the voice, and they think you just practiced really well, and you just wowed us at these auditions.'” In that moment, a confused Best was willing to do whatever’s necessary to prove he’s meant for the role. “[Watkins’] like, ‘I’m going to put you on camera and I’m going to ask you some things, and I just want you to talk back,'” the actor says. “We do that, and then he wants me to repeat some phrases, like Muhammad Ali’s favorite line, ‘I am the greatest.'” After repeating a variety of phrases, the showrunner gives Best one final line: “Jaalen, you got the role.” “I’m so locked into repeating the phrases and making sure I’m giving, I’m like, ‘Jaalen, you got the role.’ And I say it in [Muhammad’s] dialect,” he recalls. “And [Watkins’] like, ‘No, Jaalen. You got the role.’ I started to say it again, and I’m like, ‘Wait, what?’ And then they bust in, and it’s like this moment.” The Greatest Prime Video Before Best could fully celebrate, he had to get one more blessing from Muhammad’s wife, Lonnie Ali, before officially stepping into the ring. After meeting her in Louisville, Kentucky, a nervous Best was on the flight home when he “got a text from Ben basically saying, Lonnie sent a message saying, ‘He’s the one in more ways than you know.'” Below, Best opens up to THR about honoring Ali with his performance; the advice he got from Michael B. Jordan, who served as an executive producer on The Greatest ; and what he can’t live without. Playing such an iconic figure, how did you navigate honoring him with your performance, but also bringing your own portrayal to the screen? When I got the role, I started going down this deep dive on him, and I tried to gather my own perspective of what I believe he displayed to not just me but to the people. And people would tell me so many stories as well. Every time someone has an Ali story, I stop everything I’m doing and I listen in because I think it’s important to see how he affected people just off of one meeting, whether he just put his fist up or whether he just threw air punches at them or whatever the case is. It’s very beautiful to be able to rely on real connections that he made with people. I can’t ever be Ali, but I needed to get as close as possible to him. And it’s great because I feel like the look that I had, I’ve always grown up being told, “Hey, you remind us of a young Muhammad Ali,” and that never registered to me until I got in the training process. My body was naturally kind of shaped like his in a way. … And sometimes, I would just wear these white boots every single time I would train because he always wore his white boots. And my trainer would also give me footage to break down at night for homework. So on top of me doing all my studying, I broke down every punch and every movement and the rhythm of his bounces in the ring, and then I would be able to show up the next day and replicate all of that. So all of these things just allowed me to truly get to a place where I felt like I was embodying him and just really just showing up as him. And I started to rely on my own instincts and I would just say, “You know what? No more watching the movies, no more watching this.” Michael B. Jordan and Jaalen Best. Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Prime Video With Michael B. Jordan serving as an executive producer on the show, how much did you get to chat and learn from him? He’s a mentor for me. I call him Big Bro. He calls himself Big Bro. So it’s definitely something that has allowed me to feel much more of a personal connection to him as opposed to just business. Him looking out for me in terms of trying to make sure that I have a great, long career with incredible success. You hear him all the time say he wants the younger generation to be better than him, and he’s always coming with that energy when he comes to me, and I think that’s incredible. He’s somebody I can constantly look up to and see the greatness that he’s doing. I tell him, “Thank you for the blueprint and for showing us the way and continuing to lead us, especially as Black men who just want to be successful and help our community and just be a face of the world and the industry in a positive way and lead with great influence.” For those who are just getting to know you with your role in The Greatest , what do they need to know? I’m just a regular guy. I love just being inside, watching TV. Sometimes it’s hard to get me out of this room. I love going to parks and I love riding horses. I love doing just anything that people would say is boring. And then I just picked up tennis, so I’m learning tennis. I’m just trying to have fun. What’s something you absolutely cannot live without? I’m learning to relax a little bit on the coffee. I’ve been going a little crazy lately. I just love the taste of it so much. Sometimes I was literally, it’s so wild, two o’clock in the morning, I’m waking up and I’m processing, oh, should I chill off the coffee for tomorrow? Should I try to go the day without coffee? But I’m just constantly in this battle with myself because I feel like I sometimes would just order two different cups because I want to try a different coffee, but I don’t want to sacrifice to not get my favorite. *** The Greatest premieres Nov. 4 on Prime Video. title: Forest Whitaker Joins Rachid Bouchareb’s  ‘Boomerang Atomic’ As EP Ahead Of DOC NYC Screening
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Female-Focused Circle Fiction Orbit Project Incubator Unveils 2026 Cohort NewFilmmakers Los Angeles Sets Partnership With Mar Del Plata International Film Festival Cinema Guild Takes North America For Berlinale Title ‘My Wife Cries’ View All October 30, 2026 7:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Forest Whitaker Getty Images EXCLUSIVE : Academy Award-winning actor and producer Forest Whitaker has joined Rachid Bouchareb ’s Boomerang Atomic as an executive producer ahead of its screening at DOC NYC in November. The documentary revisits France’s first atomic bomb detonation on February 13, 1960 close to the remote town of Reggane in the heart of the Sahara Desert in Algeria , at a time when the country was still under French colonial rule. French Algerian director Bouchareb, whose 2006 drama Days of Glory was Oscar-nominated, examines the devastating consequences that continue to affect local populations and the environment more than six decades later. Related Stories Festivals 'Up Against It' Review: Antonio Banderas & Eva Birthisle In Trudie Styler's Witty Comedy About Divorced Couple Forced To Conceive Baby To Save Their Daughter - Toronto Film Festival News U.S. & Japanese Producers In Talks For Rachid Bouchareb's Algeria Majority-Backed French Nuclear Test Drama 'Reggane' Drawing exclusively on French state archives, the documentary presents the nuclear test through the images and commentary originally produced by French authorities, without contemporary narration, inviting audiences to confront both the history captured on film and the human realities left outside the frame. Watch on Deadline “I was impressed with the historical authenticity and powerful emotional impact. This important documentary made an indelible impact on me and needs to be seen,” said Whitaker. “After seeing Rachid Bouchareb’s documentary, I became aware of the human consequences of the atomic bomb testing in Algeria. Rachid has unveiled the misuse of the testing and its long-range consequences on the local populations and land. The film sheds a necessary light on the devastation and makes you think about what its usage would mean in warfare today.” Boomerang Atomic Boomerang Atomic is part of a larger body of work the filmmaker has been developing around France’s nuclear tests in the Algerian Sahara. The short documentary serves as the first chapter of this project, which will continue with Reggane, a feature film currently in development with American and Japanese co-producer s. Moving from archival documentary to fiction, the two films aim to illuminate a largely overlooked history, giving voice to the local populations, soldiers, and workers exposed to nuclear fallout and exploring the enduring consequences of the tests across generations and borders. “Through this documentary, I aim to revisit the French nuclear test in Reggane on 13 February 1960: France’s first atomic explosion on Algerian soil. This is not only about recounting a historical event, but about giving voice to the archival images of the time and their commentary, while shedding light on the health, environmental and human consequences that remain today,” said Bouchareb. The DOC NYC screening will continue a worldwide tour for Boomerang Atomic which premiered Out of Competition at the Venice Film Festival in 2025 and has played at numerous film festivals since, winning the Audience Award at the 2026 Seoul International Eco Film Festival. The film was also presented in Hiroshima by UNITAR, the United Nations Institute for Training and Research program, this summer as part of commemorations for the dropping of the world’s first deployed atomic bomb on the city on August 6, 1945. The bomb detonated close to Reggane was four times more powerful than that used on Hiroshima. Bouchareb’s exploration of the events around France’s Reggane nuclear tests intersects with his wider body of work exploring colonial memory, immigration, exile, identity, and Franco-Algerian history Aside from Days of Glory , his other award-winning films include Dust of Life (1995) and Outside the Law (2010). Bouchareb and Whitaker first connected through the former’s 2014 feature Berlinale competition film Two Men in Town. Whitaker starred as a recently released convict attempting to turnaround his life opposite Harvey Keitel as a vengeful sheriff determined to put him back inside.
