title: Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival
full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 7:37am PT Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ 16 minutes ago Sharjah Film Festival Partners With UAE’s Media Authority in Push to Assist Emerging Filmmakers 4 days ago Egyptian Cinema Eyes Its Next Act as Industry Veterans Call for Better Scripts, Wider Distribution 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Kot Kot Kot" (Courtesy of Boubaker Boukhari) The 13th edition of the UAE’s Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth is expanding its pitching platform for its second iteration. Six projects were selected this year, up from the three that took part during its inaugural program. The expansion is part of SIFF’s effort to build a pathway for emerging filmmakers beyond training and exhibition. As festival director Sheikha Jawaher bint Abdullah Al Qasimi told Variety ahead of this year’s edition, learning how to make a film is only part of the equation, “getting that film produced and seen is a completely different challenge.” This year’s projects bring together filmmakers from across the Arab world and diaspora, with the principal goal of finding financing and production partners from Sharjah and beyond. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!' Here are the six short film projects presented at this year’s pitching sessions: “The Black Hole” (Mike Mo Elsherif, U.S. Produced by JohnBen Lacy) Palestinian-American filmmaker Mike Mo Elsherif’s “The Black Hole” follows a Gazan refugee living in the U.S. who develops a mysterious illness as he searches for answers about his family in Gaza. El Sherif describes the film as a “visceral exploration of the complex ways in which our bodies store and process trauma throughout our lives, highlighting the deep connection between physical sensations and emotional experiences.” The film is part of a trilogy of shorts. The first installment, “Maqluba,” screens in the Arabic short films competition at SIFF following stops at Woodstock, BlackStar and El Gouna, while “Goodbye Habibi,” now in post-production, was financed by FilmLab Palestine, the Islamic Scholarship Fund, the Doha Film Institute and the Kentucky Arts Council. Currently in the financing stage, the project was developed through screenwriting lab The Front Porch Lab, under Louisville-based nonprofit 502 film, as well as The New Harmony Project, a writing organization. Partially privately financed, “The Black Hole” is seeking further funding in Sharjah ahead of a winter 2027 shoot in Louisville, Kentucky. Elsherif describes the project as “a psychological study of a Palestinian grappling with the heartbreak and dehumanization he witnesses every day,” and a search for healing amid the devastation of his homeland. “Kot Kot Kot” (Boubaker Boukhari, UAE) “Kot Kot Kot” follows a young girl grappling with the loss of her mother. Her father gives her a chick that she raises into a hen with which she grows deeply attached, only for it to suddenly disappear one day. The film grew from a story Boukhari’s mother told him as a child, which he had largely forgotten until his young nephew recounted it years later at a family gathering. “The emotion and wonder in his voice made me realize that this was a story worth telling again,” Boukhari tells Variety . Currently in production, the independently-produced UAE project has been self-financed and is seeking funding to complete post-production, particularly in music, sound design, sound effects and sound recording. Boukhari has also signed Tunisian co-producer Alaeddin Abou Taleb of Key Production Films, whose credits include the Tanit d’Or-winning stop-motion short “Diaspora” at the Carthage Film Festival. Completion is planned by the end of 2026. Illustrator Nadia Zilanova, whose international work includes commissions for the New York Times and publishing houses, recently joined the project to create and color the film’s backgrounds “in a distinctive visual style.” “The Last Call” (Saleh Mohammed, UAE) UAE-based filmmaker Saleh Mohammed’s “The Last Call” begins with an unexpected phone call from a number connected to a forgotten memory, sending its protagonist on an emotional journey through the past, unresolved feelings and unanswered questions. Mohammed says the film explores “the things we leave unsaid and the moments we fail to appreciate until they are gone.” The director described the visual approach of his film as “restrained,” allowing the film to reflect “on how a single moment can change a life and how we sometimes recognize the value of someone’s presence only after they are gone.” The screenplay is complete and the project is in pre-production, with location scouting underway and casting and crew assembly next. Mohammed is seeking financing and sponsorship, as well as potential co-producers and industry partners to help move the film into production. “In a world where communication is constant, genuine connection can sometimes be the thing we overlook most,” Mohammed says. He is also using SIFF to build relationships with festivals and distributors ahead of the film’s eventual release. Mohammed, who began his career as a theater actor and director, also co-stars in Khalid Al Mahmood’s “The Mangrove House,” the opening film of this year’s festival. “Lucky Shot” (Salah Al Hadhrami, Oman. Screenwriter Dalila Al-Dar’iya) Omani filmmaker Salah Al Hadhrami’s “Lucky Shot” centers on Amjad, a boy from a working-class neighborhood whose passion for football fuels dreams of a life beyond his modest circumstances. An unexpected turn of events forces him to choose between those ambitions and temptation that could change his future. Written by Omani filmmaker, writer and actor Dalila Al-Dar’iya, the 12-15 minute narrative short is in development, with initial approaches made to potential cast members. The independent project has yet to secure production financing and is seeking backers and co-producers in Sharjah and elsewhere in the region, with a tentative 2027 shoot dependent on funding. “I believe that simple stories can carry the profoundest human messages,” Al Hadhrami says. For the director, the film is less about football itself than the moment when an unexpected opportunity becomes “a true test.” The goal, above all, Al Hadhrami shares, is “to tell an authentic story that transcends geographical and cultural boundaries, one that resonates with the audience’s emotions. We hope to find partners who believe in this message and will help bring the film to the screen.” “My Uncle Saman” (“Saman 3my”) (Aljouri Abdelaziz Alzarooni, UAE. Creative Producer Shahad Al Ali) Emirati writer-director Aljouri Abdelaziz Alzarooni’s “My Uncle Saman” follows three young men on their way to their uncle’s long-awaited wedding. The groom, who is close enough in age to feel more like a cousin, sends them on a quick errand that turns into a string of misadventures, leaving the trio at risk of missing the wedding altogether. The comedy short is in development and has yet to secure financing or attach a production company. Alzarooni is seeking financing and production partners at SIFF, along with collaborators in areas including cinematography, sound and post-production. She says the pitch has already generated interest from potential partners, with discussions now underway. The young director says potential partners expressed strong enthusiasm for the project’s “fresh and distinctive approach to Emirati storytelling.” “‘My Uncle Saman’ is rooted in the natural humour, relationships, and everyday experiences of Emirati families, and I want to bring that authenticity to the screen in a way that audiences everywhere can connect with,” Alzarooni says. Alzarooni is also eyeing eventual support from potential distributors, broadcasters, streaming platforms and industry mentors as her search to secure financing continues. “Tomato Merchant” (Thoraya Farzaneh, UAE. Produced by Sayed Mousavi) UAE-based filmmaker Thoraya Farzaneh makes her directing debut with “Tomato Merchant,” about an elderly man who spends his day selling tomatoes in a quiet neighborhood and refuses to leave until they are all sold. As repeated attempts are made to persuade him to go home, the reason for the insistence gradually becomes clear. Farzaneh, who has spent the past several years working as an assistant director and writing scripts, says she waited until she felt ready to direct a story of her own. “I feel this is the right moment to take that step and share one of my stories with the world.” The independent short has received funding from the RAK Art Fund, supported by the Sharjah-based Al Qasimi Foundation, while FANN – Media Discovery Platform, the parent organization of the festival, will provide post-production support following its SIFF pitch. Now in pre-production, “Tomato Merchant” is set to shoot in the UAE in early November, with completion targeted for January. Farzaneh is using SIFF to explore festival and distribution opportunities for the finished film. Producer Sayed Mousavi says, “This film reminds us that kindness often begins with the simple choice to be patient.” “Tomato Merchant” Courtesy of Thoraya Farzaneh Charli xcx Cancels ‘Music, Fashion, Film’ Show in Arizona Due to Illness: ‘It Breaks Me That I Can’t Be With You’ Charli xcx Announces U.K. and Europe ‘Music, Fashion, Film’ Tour Dates, With Audrey Hobert Opening Charli xcx Brings Out Chappell Roan for ‘Boom Clap’ at Los Angeles Concert Madonna Opens MTV Video Music Awards With Sabrina Carpenter and Charli xcx, Plus Sombr, Debi Mazar and More Elton John, Charli xcx, Burna Boy and More Set Shows at New Apple Music Hall in London Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese’s ‘What Happens at Night’ With Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

title: Goldman Sachs Thinks the Sports Boom Isn’t Going Anywhere
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 7:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jaydon Blue of the Dallas Cowboys rushes against the Arizona Cardinals during the preseason NFL game at State Farm Stadium on Aug. 22 in Glendale, Arizona. Christian Petersen/Getty Images Within most media companies, sports remain core to their larger content strategy. Premium entertainment isn’t going anywhere, of course, but if you ask Ted Sarandos or Mike Cavanagh or Josh D’Amaro about their content mix, sports will be at the center of it. “These events break through,” Sarandos said on the company’s last earnings call. “They drive new membership, they add fuel to our ad revenues.” It’s with that backdrop that Goldman Sachs is releasing a new report focused on sports investing … and the bank is predicting that the sports economy is only going to go up from here. “We increasingly hear from our clients a continuation of a theme that started with our first paper two years ago, which is this really high level of interest in participating in this explosion that we’re seeing in the sports ecosystem,” says Goldman Sachs partner Nicole Pullen Ross. “When you think about the trajectory of growth within sports, our expectation is that we’ll see growth within the sports ecosystem grow to you know over $600 billion by 2030, that’s 44 percent growth.” Indeed, the new Goldman report notes a number of things contributing to that explosive growth, from continually rising media rights deals (the bank estimates global sports media rights will hit $67 billion this year); institutional capital buying into teams; and all the ancillary opportunities around entertainment and live events and IP. “Streaming is now 20 percent of the market for media rights and those contributions of how advertisers are thinking about reaching the consumer in a real-time way is one of the drivers of what we’re seeing,” Ross says. “We’re very analytical in terms of thinking about the value and what the data suggests. One of the things that we saw was the expectation that media rights growth would continue, and the participation was becoming much broader in terms of in terms of the value of the consumer and that live entertainment part of the formula.” Goldman also dug into some more sector-wide (and in some cases economywide) trends: Institutional investors are buying into teams as league change their roles to give owners more liquidity, and sports team owners, like many business owners, are exploring how artificial intelligence can improve efficiency and create more personalized fan experiences. But the report also digs into the ancillary opportunities in sports, particularly around athlete-centric brands (athlete-led studios and consumer brands, etc) shortform content, and opportunities like VR tickets to games. “In an increasingly fragmented media landscape, sports owners are leveraging the power of storytelling to capture and retain a fan base with an increasingly short attention span,” the report states. “Rather than relying solely on traditional broadcasts, they use narrative-driven content to sustain the appeal of live games while capturing younger demographics.” “When you consider the brands that the athletes have and the longevity of their lives post-career, there is an opportunity one for the athlete to want to invest in their brand and those relationships while they’re still playing, but also the opportunity for them to transition that into areas of focus for their business interests,” Ross says. “So the creativity is around how can we make the athlete more relatable? How can we get more fans to engage? Particularly the younger audience, and how can we use technology as a way to do that? Some of the shortform engagement is an example of that, and so that creativity around making additional ways available to increase engagement and participation is one of the things that we heard from clients and the creativity that they’re using to to make sure that they are having points of differentiated connectivity across their across their attendee base. ultimately, teams want to win, owners want to win.” THR

title: Eric Karson, Director of ‘The Octagon’ and Producer of ‘Lionheart,’ Dies at 86
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 6:41am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Director Eric Karson at work on 1980’s ‘The Octagon.’ American Cinema Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection Eric Karson, the martial-arts movie specialist who directed Chuck Norris in The Octagon and produced the Jean-Claude Van Damme-starring Lionheart , has died. He was 86. Karson died Aug. 24 of natural causes while in hospice care in Henderson, Nevada, his brother Gil Karson told The Hollywood Reporter . Karson also directed Olivier Gruner in his first movie, Angel Town (1990), and produced his second film, Nemesis (1992), and the French kickboxer considered Karson a mentor. Related Stories Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist Movies Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies at 86 The son of a TV writer, Karson was working for Los Angeles-based American Cinema Productions when he was offered the chance to make his feature directorial debut on The Octagon (1980). Written by Leigh Chapman of Dirty Mary Crazy Larry fame at the dawn of the ninja movie craze, the film stars Norris as Scott James, a retired karate champion who takes on a band of assassins led by his estranged foster brother (Tadashi Yamashita). At Imperial Entertainment, Karson directed Van Damme in Black Eagle (1988), then reunited with the Belgian martial artist on Lionheart (1990), directed by Sheldon Lettich. With his turn as Lyon Gaultier, who deserts the French Foreign Legion and becomes a street fighter to raise money for his murdered brother’s family, Van Damme became a leading man in the U.S. One of four kids, Karson was born in Phoenix on March 5, 1940. His father was Lee Karson, who created the 1956-59 CBS-ABC program The Gale Storm Show (also known as Oh, Susanna ), set on a ship à la The Love Boat ; he also wrote for shows including The Restless Gun , Wagon Train and The Detectives . His mother, Mary, was a theater actress turned homemaker. The family moved to L.A. in the 1950s and lived in a house next door to John Wayne on Highland Avenue in Hancock Park. Karson, who started out as an actor, graduated from Cal State Northridge and began his directing career on commercials and documentaries in Australia. Back in L.A., he handled spots for The Peterson Co., a leading production house back then, and served as a vp before getting his big break on The Octagon . Karson also directed the action flick Opposing Force (1986), starring Lisa Eichhorn and Tom Skerritt , and appeared onscreen as a CIA chief in Black Eagle and as a doctor in Lionheart . In addition to his brother, a musician who also has worked as a film editor, survivors include his other siblings, Lisa and Michael; his wife of two decades, Tara; his nieces, Sylvia and Jackie Lee; and his nephew, Josh. THR

title: Christina Hendricks, Accidental DJ, Has Music Lovers Lining Up
full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All October 30, 2026 6:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source DJ Christina Hendricks at Sid's Bar. Eric Garcia The queue outside of the auditorium snaked nearly 200 people long. This wasn’t an unusual sight for the South Pasadena concert hall from bookers and promoters Sid the Cat. Their year-old destination, housed inside a 19th Century elementary school, has already hosted Sylvan Esso, Mike D, Death Cab for Cutie and Jenny Lewis side hustle Nice as Fuck. But on the October Saturday in question, the stage was empty. Instead, the crowd was there for actress Christina Hendricks at the venue’s bar. Most would expect Hendricks, the instantly recognizable redhead from Mad Men , Drive and Good Girls , to be there performing a one-woman show. Maybe some experimental theater. Perhaps she’s just joined the legion of celebrities with their own line of spirits. But they clearly don’t know Hendricks, because she was there to DJ. “Everyone who knows me says, ‘Oh yeah, this makes perfect sense,’” Hendricks tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Because I’ve been doing this since junior high, making playlists and forcing them upon people. This is my favorite thing.” Related Stories Movies 'Ancestors' Invites You to a Cinematic "Séance," Led by Éanna Hardwicke, That Mixes Dream, Reality and Memory (Exclusive TIFF Clip and Chat) TV Naomie Harris and Christina Hendricks Filming BBC Legal Drama 'Reputation' Rumblings of “DJ Christina Hendricks” began earlier in 2026 after she made two appearances at San Diego listening bar Part Time Lover. Her debut was a bit of a fluke at the coaxing of her close friend, the harpist and DJ Mary Lattimore. She suggested Hendricks bring some of her own records down from Los Angeles. She’d show her the ropes and they’d share billing. Hendricks says she balked for a split second before she recognized the kind of wish fulfillment that was on the table. Each played for two hours. Hendricks proved a quick study and Part Time Lover asked her back. But with Lattimore busy, she decided to go it alone. She was getting comfortable with the gear, and it felt like a relatively low-pressure scenario. Hendricks at Sid’s Bar. (Photo credit: Eric Garcia ) “When we started walking towards the venue, my husband went, ‘I think there’s a line out front,’” says Hendricks, who’s married to cinematographer George Bianchini. “I said, ‘Oh no, sweetie, that must be for restaurants and stuff.’ As we got closer, he was like, ‘No, I’m pretty sure that’s a line for you.’ That’s when I started feeling pressure.” If she’s still feeling pressure, it appears to be eclipsed by the kick she’s getting out of all of this. At Sid’s Bar, a former classroom in the 140-year-old building, Hendricks looked gleeful as she navigated a playlist that meandered between Shoegaze, Chillwave, Electronic and Indie Sleeze. The crowd, which appeared to lean heavy on 30-to-50-somethings, nodded in approval. And when Hendricks transitioned from Washed Out to The Knife, this geriatric millennial, for one, felt very seen. The free show marked Hendricks’ first gig in Los Angeles County, so the audience naturally skewed a little industry. Mad Men creator Matthew Weiner was in the crowd, as was Hendricks’ longtime body double and stand-in, Becky Stockton. Johnny Jewel, the artist and music producer who scored Hendricks vehicle Lost River , was there, as were colleagues of Bianchini. Many filtered in and out during the four-hour set, though the bar remained at capacity until she closed with “Protest Song” by Broken Social Scene. Hendricks says she’s still getting used to different crowds and isn’t sure what to think when people don’t dance. “I’m trying to not let how people react determine whether they had a good time or not,” she says. “As an actor, hopefully you’re making people feel something and telling a story. But it’s someone else’s story. With this, I’m not just the performer but the director and the editor at the same time. I’m in the room with the audience, so they’re a part of it as well. I’ve realized that it’s just a different way to tell a story.” Attendees and a few lookie-loos at Hendricks’ set. (Photo credit: Eric Garcia ) Recently wrapping two acting projects — the third season of Apple TV+ drama The Buccaneers and BBC miniseries Reputation , in which she stars opposite Naomie Harris — Hendricks says she’s leaning into DJing as much as she can. On Halloween, she’ll return to San Diego for another set at Part Time Lover. And, throughout November, she’ll be part of a guest DJ series on KCRW, programming an hour of music each week. For the first two weeks, which she’d already submitted when we spoke, her intention is to stick to what she’s been spinning live. Then she plans to stretch herself a little more. A “sad girl dreamy hour,” an A guitar-focused set and a dark, moody jazz playlist are all on the table. When I remind Hendricks that it’s almost awards season and invites for her to DJ Hollywood parties are probably already being drafted, she says she’s game. “I’d love that,” says Hendricks. “The nice thing about all of this is that each time I do it, I get more calls — offers to come and do stuff, people saying they’ll help teach me new things — and I’m saying yes. Let’s do it all.” THR

title: Female-Focused Circle Fiction Orbit Project Incubator Unveils 2026 Cohort
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Female-Focused Circle Fiction Orbit Project Incubator Unveils 2026 Cohort NewFilmmakers Los Angeles Sets Partnership With Mar Del Plata International Film Festival Cinema Guild Takes North America For Berlinale Title ‘My Wife Cries’ View All October 30, 2026 5:39am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Circle Fiction Orbit participants Circle EXCLUSIVE: The Circle Training Initiative, dedicated to women and gender-expansive filmmakers, has unveiled the five feature film projects selected for its third Circle Fiction Orbit incubator event taking place in Montenegro this week. They include Portuguese director and screenwriter Leonor Bettencourt Loureiro’s Por Este Arroios Acima , exploring the connection between the rapid transformation of the body, city and community building in the aftermath of a traumatic accident. It is the director’s second fiction feature after C’est Pas la Vie en Rose, which tapped into the zeitgeist of contemporary Lisbon as longtime residents grapple with implications of gentrification. Rita de Moura Santos at Grumpy Panda Productions is producing. Related Stories News Circle Kicks Off Inaugural Fiction Program With Nukâka Coster Waldau & Pipaluk Jørgensen Among Participants News Russell Brand Rape Trial: Channel 4 Film Was Not "Magic Force" That Caused Accusers To "Recast" Memories, Court Hears In Closing Arguments Georgian director and screenwriter Irine Jordania is participating with Tbilisi-set Nutsa.Love revolving around the unfolding relationship between an unlikely couple. It is her second feature after Air Blue Silk which premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival. She is joined by producer Elene Margvelashvili. Watch on Deadline The selection also features Dutch director Sabine Lubbe Bakker’s Premier Souffle , exploring whether a rebellious outsider can find her place in the world after years of isolation from her community. It is produced by Baldr Film. The director’s 2020 film Becoming Mona travelled the festival circuit. Montenegrin director and producer Katarina Bulajić is participating with first feature project Leech , about a woman returning to her hometown who is confronted by the magnitude of betrayal. Bulajić latest short film A Special Day is currently on the festival circuit and due to screen at Germany’s FilmFestival Cottbus next week. She is joined by screenwriter and producer Ana Vujadinovic at Montenegrin company Giggling Goat Production. The selection also includes Polish director and screenwriter Marta Prus’ drama Soloist , exploring the elite world of ballet and reinvention of the body and soul at the end of a career and beginning of something new. It follows Prus’ award-winning documentary Over The Limit about Russian gymnast and Olympic gold medalist Margarita Mamun. The new film is produced by Telemark. The lineup, focused on mid-career filmmakers and teams, was selected by a three-person committee consisting of writer and producer Suzy Gillet, film scholar Jelena Mišeljić and writer and director Ivana Mladenović. They were guided by Circle Head of Programme Biljana Tutorov – writer, director and producer of To Hold A Mountain , which is currently shortlisted for the European Film Award – and Circle Co-Head of Programme Brigid O’Shea. The seven-day residential project development retreat is currently underway in Herceg Novi, Montenegro and runs until November 1. It is led by award-winning producer and screenwriter Bianca Oana ( Touch Me Not , Collective , Anhell69 ). “This is a rare opportunity for filmmakers and producers to come together, to think and exchange experiences outside the norms and the excruciating pulse of the industry,” said Oana. “We make space to reflect not only on the films we want to make, but also on how we want to make them. Urgency and immediacy give way to listening and care. This slow time is the real time of cinema, where projects can grow into films.” She is joined by producers Myriam Sassine ( Costa Brava Lebanon) , Dana Bunescu ( The Death of Mr Lazarescu ) and Dominique Welinski, founder of the world cinema focused Next Steps Studio taking place within the framework of Cannes Critics’ Week. The programme also features a keynote session with Dea Kulumbegashvili and screening of her Venice Special Jury Prize-winning film April. “Circle Fiction Orbit is our cherished space for filmmakers working to reach the next level of their careers,” said Tutorov. “Dedicated to filmmakers, this mission informs every aspect of our methodology and framework: from the curation of mentors, experts and screenings to the location of Herceg Novi and led by Bianca Oana’s unique approach to activate their potential and find a new dynamic, all contributes to creating and environment conductive to holistic project development.” Three projects from the first two editions have come to fruition and are travelling the festival circuit: Lex Julia by director Laura Hyppönen which will compete for Best Baltic Film in Tallinn in November; IDDA , directed by Irene Dionisio, which world in Toronto and Perla by Alexandra Makarová (Austria and Slovakia) which played in Rotterdam. Founded in 2018, Circle was built to support women and gender-expansive filmmakers. It is co-funded by Creative Europe MEDIA and organised under the patronage of Eurimage by Wake Up Films. title: Russell Brand Rape Trial: Channel 4 Film Was Not “Magic Force” That Caused Accusers To “Recast” Memories, Court Hears In Closing Arguments
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake AI Dubbing Pioneer Flawless Sells Technology In Deal That Raises Questions About Its Future Russell Brand’s Wife Says Star Was “Caring” Lover At Time Of Rape Allegations BAFTA Launches Review Over Concerns About Trustees Accepting Free Awards Guest Tickets View All October 30, 2026 5:26am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand arrives in court this week Getty Editor’s note: T his story contains details of alleged sexual offenses that some readers may find distressing . Channel 4’s 2023 exposé on Russell Brand was not a “magic force” that caused six separate women to “recast” their memories and accuse the Despicable Me star of rape and sexual assault, a court has heard. Related Stories News Prosecution Rejects Russell Brand’s Claim He Has Been Abandoned: “You Have A Platform Of Millions” Legal Russell Brand’s Wife Says Star Was “Caring” Lover At Time Of Rape Allegations Riel Karmy-Jones, the prosecution barrister, presented her closing arguments to the jury at London’s Southwark Crown Court, where Brand is on trial over three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one of attempted indecent assault. Deadline has been reporting daily on the trial from a live video feed of the courtroom. Karmy-Jones began her closing remarks by reminding the jury that the six women behind the seven charges are “wholly unconnected” insofar as they “do not know each other and have never met.” She continued: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not taken part in documentaries, who have not made claims for compensation … There is no benefit to them.” Watch on Deadline Karmy-Jones said Russell Brand: In Plain Sight , the 2023 Channel 4 documentary, and reporting by The Times of London , had caused the women — who have a lifelong right to anonymity — to come forward and tell stories about their encounters with Brand that had “haunted them for years.” Karmy-Jones rejected Brand’s defense that the documentary was “evil and untrue” and “caused them to recast what actually happened.” She asked: “Could a documentary or Times article have such sway over perfectly rational women? Could a documentary cause them to completely reinvent what happened?” Karmy-Jones argued there was no “magic force” and “woo-woo” in the film. Instead, she said the “women have realized they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth.” “They have vivid recollections of what took place,” the prosecution lawyer said, and “were not moved from their accounts” under cross-examination from defense barrister Ian Winter. In contrast, Karmy-Jones said Brand remembers very little of the women and manipulated his account after reading the prosecution’s case. In legal directions to the jury earlier on Friday, Mr Justice Bennathan, the judge presiding over the trial, told the jury to disregard the Channel 4 documentary when coming to their decision. “Do not think that a few women making anonymous complaints in a TV show adds any support at all to the prosecution,” he said. “The defendant denied the allegations [in the documentary] in robust, detailed terms. They were never tested in any court.” Bennathan said the jury must reach unanimous verdicts on each of the charges to convict Brand. He reminded jurors that the burden of proof is on the prosecution and that Brand is entitled to the benefit of the doubt. Bennathan expects the jury to begin verdict deliberations next Tuesday, November 3. The trial continues. title: Edinburgh Film Festival Toasts Bollywood With ‘Kuch Kuch Hota Hai’ Anniversary Event at 2028 Edition
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 3:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kajol, Shahrukh Khan in 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' Courtesy of Everett Bollywood is coming to the Edinburgh International Film Festival . EIFF on Friday confirmed that a special 30th anniversary celebration of the legendary Indian film Kuch Kuch Hota Hai (1998) will screen as part of the 2028 edition. Partly filmed in Scotland, the beloved cult favorite — and Karan Johar’s directorial debut, following the love triangle between Rahul Khanna ( Shah Rukh Khan ), Anjali Sharma ( Kajol ) and Tina Malhotra (Rani Mukerji) — will return to the cinema to celebrate its enduring legacy as a landmark of Indian cinema, with Johar and other guests in attendance. Related Stories Movies From 'Sh*t Happens' to an Erotic Photographer Being Confronted by His Daughter: Offbeat Films at Tallinn Movies Jamie Dornan Boards 'Nostalgie,' Starring Aidan Gillen as Washed-up Pop Star, as Executive Producer (Exclusive) Johar was invited to mark Kuch Kuch Hota Hai ‘s anniversary at the 2028 EIFF during a meeting he hosted in the Mumbai offices of his production company, Dharma Productions, earlier this week with the First Minister of Scotland, John Swinney, and Screen Scotland’s interim executive director, David Smith. The meeting, said EIFF, was focused on Scotland’s potential as a destination and partner for Indian film and television production, co-production, talent development and cultural exchange. Kuch Kuch Hota Hai was the first major Indian production to film extensively across Scotland, including Eilean Donan Castle, Glen Coe, Tantallon Castle and Inchmahome Priory. Swinney said: “It was a pleasure to meet Karan Johar in Mumbai […] I look forward to welcoming him to Edinburgh. During my visit to India, I met with people from the Indian film industry, including representatives from Dharma Productions, to discuss opportunities for future collaboration between Scottish and Indian filmmaking. Scotland’s screen industry has tremendous potential as a creative partner for Indian film and television, offering the infrastructure, expertise and world-class filming locations to support a wide range of productions.” EIFF CEO and festival director Paul Ridd said his team is always thinking about the future and what’s next. “So we jumped at an opportunity like this,” he said, “to plant the seeds for a celebration of a legendary, much-loved film at our festival, a film featuring Scotland and some of the most iconic stars of Bollywood cinema on screen. We can’t wait for what promises to be something truly special for our 81st edition in 2028. But in the meantime, watch this space for more news of our 80th next August.” The 80th Edinburgh International Film Festival is set to run Aug. 12-18. THR

title: From ‘Sh*t Happens’ to an Erotic Photographer Being Confronted by His Daughter: Offbeat Films at Tallinn
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 30, 2026 2:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'The Two Hornets' Courtesy of PÖFF The 30th anniversary edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) is kicking off on Nov. 6, screening all sorts of art house world premieres, new discoveries and highlights from the festival circuit of the past year. Movies from the Baltic region, Europe, Asia and beyond will screen in the Estonian capital and look to create buzz. Among the titles are some that at first glance sound particularly offbeat, even edgy or outlandish. After all, the programming team likes to offer up cinematic experiences that go beyond the mainstream and the safe. Related Stories Movies Jamie Dornan Boards 'Nostalgie,' Starring Aidan Gillen as Washed-up Pop Star, as Executive Producer (Exclusive) Movies 'Godzilla Minus Zero': First Reactions With all that in mind, THR has compiled a look at some of the more unusual-sounding films unspooling at PÖFF 2026 below. Sinless Director: Attila Hartung Section: Official Competition Hungarian director Hartung premiered his 2019 feature debut, FOMO, at Tallinn. Now, he returns with the world premiere of Sinless , which sounds like a tension-filled mix of The Godfather and Thanksgiving. The director co-wrote the psychological thriller with horror novelist Attila Veres, so we likely want to get ready for a feast of menacing posing and fear. And it sounds like there are generations of crimes to uncover for a young man. But is he the hunter or the hunted? ‘Sinless’ film still, courtesy of PÖFF “Henrik (Márk Nagy) arrives at the Szentiványi family’s castle for a celebratory dinner,” a synopsis starts off rather calmly. “Wine fills the glasses, and Hungary’s powerful construction dynasty welcomes him into its carefully ordered world.” But wait, here comes the thriller element! Henrik is no ordinary guest. “Only Anita (Anna Mészöly), his girlfriend and the family’s youngest daughter, suspects why he’s there,” the synopsis continues. “For generations, the Szentiványis have moved through the highest political and economic circles, leaving crimes and unspoken debts in their wake. As the evening unfolds, casual remarks sharpen, silences deepen, and every polished courtesy seems to carry another meaning. … At this table, innocence may be the most carefully rehearsed role of all.” If you are up for an appetizer and have nerves of steel, here’s the trailer. The Two Hornets Director: Dominik György Section: Rebels With a Cause Competition The PÖFF website describes Slovakian director György’s feature debut as a solo director as a “daring queer story” and a “diverse, vibrant, chic, and quirky love and revenge thriller.” It even suggests that the creator has been influenced by Xavier Dolan, whose Mommy was shot in the same 1:1 square format that The Two Hornets is presented in. Now get ready for the synopsis of this Tallinn world premiere: “Samo, a gay man facing an unplanned pregnancy with a woman overseas, reunites with his narcissistic mother at a remote forest cabin to confront their toxic past. Amidst a drug-fueled sexual affair with his former childhood bully, he struggles to decide if he should embrace fatherhood or break the cycle of inherited family sin.” ‘The Two Hornets’ Courtesy of PÖFF So far, so wild and so rated R, you say!? Wait for the kicker that less patient viewers may want to know about, given the movie’s running time of 3 hours and 8 minutes. In Samo’s warped reality, omnipresent hornets gain an evil power, forcing him to confront his mother in what could turn into a brutal showdown. By the way: György could well target new records for multihyphenates. He not only wrote and directed The Two Hornets , but also produced it, handled cinematography and editing – plus, he has the music credit on the film. If you still need help to figure out if this one’s for you, check out a trailer here. Crocodile Directors: Pietra Brettkelly, The Critics Section: Doc@Just Sticking with an animal theme for now, PÖFF’s Youth and Children’s Film Festival has some eyebrow-raising films on offer this year. One of them is Crocodile , which the fest website promotes this way: “A documentary about young Nigerians whose amateur sci-fi films have been praised even by the creator of Star Wars !” No, not George Lucas. But J.J. Abrams acknowledged their “brilliant, inventive” work and rallied Bad Robot’s Kate Webster to send the team a crate packed with professional filmmaking gear, cameras, and laptops. The Critics is a collective of young filmmakers based in Kaduna, Nigeria, made up of friends and family members. And the crew has been making movies since childhood – with a phone, self-built sets and much imagination – even though power outages and everyday struggles may interfere with their work. ‘Crocodile,’ courtesy of PÖFF Courtesy of PÖFF “Over the years, their films begin to reach an international audience, forcing The Critics to face new opportunities, but also the challenges that come with responsibility,” the PÖFF website notes. New Zealand filmmaker Pietra Brettkelly collaborated with the young creative team on Crocodile , which premiered at Berlin and is now bringing their DIY filmmaking spirit to Tallinn. Check out the trailer. Love Exposed Director: Filip Remunda Section: Doc@PÖFF International Competition If you think that your family is complicated, just read the logline for this documentary, which is getting its world premiere at the Estonian festival: “He’s spent a lifetime photographing naked women. Now his daughter wants him to reveal himself.” Blanka, a successful film editor, confronts her father, Vlastimil Kula, about his career as an “erotic photographer.” Teases a synopsis: “What follows is a series of encounters exploring her childhood, her father’s provocative legacy and decades of buried family history. The film captures a world that is eccentric, hilarious, uncomfortable and deeply touching, sometimes all at the same time, as Blanka attempts to understand their shared past and find a way to connect before it’s too late.” ‘Love Exposed’ film still – PÖFF – H 2026 The doc, filmed over four years, “takes an intimate, observational approach, getting up close to his characters and capturing brutally frank conversations, moments of vulnerability and unexpected tenderness,” the PÖFF website notes. “The film slowly reveals the layers of Kula, a man more comfortable with nudity than emotional openness.” Love Exposed comes from Czech doc maker Remunda, whose previous films have such titles as Czech Dream , which explored consumerism and media manipulation, Czech Peace , and Happiness to All , about a Russian vlogger, patriotic activist and record holder in cold water swimming who is gradually changing his mind about Putin’s Russia. Here’s a trailer for his new film. Dice-Ching-O-Mat Director: Kristijonas Vildziunas Section: Baltic Film Competition How’s this for a pitch? Yasujirō Ozu meets Christopher Nolan, and the ancient Chinese Book of Changes , the I Ching , meets retro sci-fi, with Lithuanian flavor added for an unusual mix. Welcome to Dice-Ching-O-Mat ! Dainius Gavenonis ( Johatsu , The Southern Chronicles ) stars as Vilis, a 55-year-old professor of Asian studies who has spent so much of his life focused on work that he has grown distant from his wife and three children and even forgotten their health problems. ‘Dice-Ching-O-Mat’ film still – PÖFF – H 2026 Now, he wakes up inside an elevator-like cube filled with an old TV set, a mysterious intercom, and riddles, such as “Who are you?” And he must roll dice to get a chance to go through moments from the life he has been too busy to notice. Oh yeah, and he must find the green door before it is too late. In Lithuanian director Vildziunas’ ( Songs for a Fox , Seneca’s Day ) sixth feature, which recently premiered at the Warsaw International Film Festival , philosophical and sci-fi riddles may prove not to be as hard to solve as the mystery of human connection. Watch the Dice-Ching-O-Mat trailer here. Sh*t Happens Director: José María Cabral Section: Official Competition You may mainly think of the Dominican Republic as a great destination for a holiday. But you may want to think again when you hear about the dark comedy cinematic export it is bringing to Tallinn for its world premiere. Flush away all the negativity and potty like a rockstar with Sh*t Happens ! “When science fails, trust your gut. Just don’t ask what the ‘miracle cure’ is made of,” reads a logline for the new film from Cabral, who has seen three of his films submitted for the best international feature film Oscar race, namely The Projectionist , an homage to pre-digital cinema as seen through the lens of an old-style traveling cinema owner, Woodpeckers , about an impossible romance between inmates at adjacent male and female prisons, and the thriller Checkmate . ‘Sh*t Happens’ film still – PÖFF – H 2026 In case you haven’t noticed yet, this movie is different. It tells the story of the people in a wealthy Dominican household. “Verónica (Lizbeth Santos) controls every bite eaten by her sickly daughter Isabella, while Raúl (Fele Martínez), a frustrated biotechnologist, experiments with homemade cures. Only Abi (Cindy Galán), the young nanny, can still make the girl smile,” explains a synopsis. “Then Raúl develops a microbiotic treatment with a secret ingredient as astonishing as its results. Isabella’s gut stabilizes, her strength returns – and soon the household’s other illnesses begin clearing up too.” And word spreads. A remedy nobody can quite explain becomes the one thing everyone wants. But then the miracle takes an unexpected turn. You are likely smelling that you are in for a very different game of thrones. The trailer only gives you a minimal tease for the film. Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag Director: Vesa Kuosmanen Section: Doc@PÖFF International Competition Finnish filmmaker Kuosmanen’s documentary Just Animals , which screened at Tallinn in 2023, is a portrait of an animal rights activist facing her own limits when she realizes that the utopia she has always fought for will never quite be as she imagined. His new doc also features compelling real-life characters and also has a provocative title, Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag . But it focuses on a very different story – one of a community’s cultural memory. ‘Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag,’ courtesy of PÖFF Courtesy of PÖFF Jolanda, a retired archivist, stood on a stage in the late 1970s alongside his friend Mummo in Finland’s first drag show, Happy Gays , which drew much attention and big audiences. Mummo was one of the first openly gay men in Finland, but then the AIDS crisis hit, causing fear and violence. In 1988, Mummo was killed in his home. More than 30 years later, Jolanda opens up his own archive and invites a new generation of drag artists to bring Happy Gays back to the stage. The re-enactments bring up painful memories, but also an inappropriate and humorous side of Jolanda. The film mixes archive footage from the 1980s, staged reconstructions and contemporary footage from rehearsals featuring young people for whom drag is more a form of self-expression than for the pioneers. “This contrast gives rise to both humor and a sense of recognition,” the PÖFF website teases. “The freedom enjoyed by today’s youth has been built on the shoulders of people whom no one has ever thanked. This warm and heartfelt film … reminds us that Pride began, in part, out of fear, and that one small show was once a tiny step towards resistance and freedom.” The Mystery Package Director: Silje Evensno Jacobsen Section: Doc@Just With that time of year nearing, PÖFF is also serving up a slice of holiday season spirit in the form of a mystery package. Well, actually, The Mystery Package . The cinematic surprise comes courtesy of Norwegian filmmaker Silje Evensno Jacobsen, who you can actually see in the documentary. ‘The Mystery Package,’ courtesy of PÖFF It’s not a mystery what the film is about. Just take a look at this synopsis: “Nine-year-old Edle and six-year-old Brage have racked their brains their whole lives: why has their family been receiving a bunch of strange presents every Christmas from an anonymous sender for the past 20 years? With their filmmaker mother and close relatives, who are all, naturally, suspects themselves, the children become fearless detectives.” What will they encounter on their unusual but heart-warming journey? “They leave no ink-stained handwriting unchecked, no suspicious person uninterrogated, no post office security footage unwatched, and no snowball unturned,” the festival website promises. That leaves one key question to be answered: “Will the anonymous benefactor be found before Christmas is over?” While you wait for the answer, check out the trailer for The Mystery Package . THR
